title: QMA(2) with Limited Shared Entanglement
abstract: A $\mathsf{QMA}(2)$ protocol involves two provers submitting unentangled witnesses to a polynomial-time quantum verifier. In The Power of Unentanglement (ToC, 2009), Aaronson et al. proposed $\mathsf{QMA}(2;h)$, a variant of $\mathsf{QMA}(2)$ in which the two provers may share $h$ EPR pairs. Our main result shows that the power of $\mathsf{QMA}(2)$ remains unchanged for up to logarithmically many shared EPR pairs: $\mathsf{QMA}(2;h)=\mathsf{QMA}(2)$ for $h=O(\log n)$, where $n$ is the input length. The result follows from a simulation using four unentangled witnesses, combined with the Harrow-Montanaro equality $\mathsf{QMA}(4)=\mathsf{QMA}(2)$ (FOCS, 2010).   We also prove monotonicity in the EPR budget: $\mathsf{QMA}(2;h)\subseteq\mathsf{QMA}(2;H)$ for $h\le H$, preserving completeness and soundness. Combined with input padding, this shows that establishing $\mathsf{QMA}(2;n^\varepsilon)=\mathsf{QMA}(2)$ for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$ would imply equality for every polynomially bounded budget, resolving the open problem raised by Aaronson et al.   Finally, we extend these results to a variant of the model in which the provers may use local operations and classical communication (LOCC) during witness preparation. For logarithmic-size witnesses and inverse-polynomial gaps, both models remain equivalent to their unentangled counterpart when $h=O(\log n)$. We show that extending this equivalence to any superlogarithmic EPR budget in the LOCC model would imply $\mathsf{NP}\subseteq\mathsf{BQP}$.
summary: This paper rigorously analyzes the robustness of the QMA(2) complexity class against limited shared entanglement, showing that sharing only a logarithmic number of EPR pairs does not increase the computational power. The findings resolve an open problem regarding polynomial entanglement budgets and establish a critical threshold: exceeding logarithmic entanglement in certain models implies a major collapse ($	ext{NP} \subseteq 	ext{BQP}$).
main_problem: The paper investigates how the computational power of the QMA(2) complexity class is affected when the two provers are allowed to share a limited amount of entanglement, quantified by $h$ shared EPR pairs.
main_result: The power of QMA(2) remains unchanged even when the provers share a logarithmic number of EPR pairs ($h=O(\log n)$), and establishing this for polynomial budgets would resolve an open problem in the field.
method: The analysis uses techniques involving simulating QMA(2; h) within QMA(4) using four unentangled witnesses, combined with monotonicity proofs and padding arguments.
model_or_system: The model is the QMA(2) protocol, where two provers submit quantum witnesses to a quantum verifier. The resource being studied is the shared entanglement, modeled by $h$ EPR pairs, leading to the class $	ext{QMA}(2; h)$.
key_observables: The acceptance probability of the quantum verifier, the gap ($\gamma$) between completeness and soundness thresholds, and the required entanglement budget ($h$).
important_parameters: Input length $n$, entanglement budget $h$, and the fixed constant $\epsilon$ used in polynomial padding arguments.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the Harrow-Montanaro equality ($	ext{QMA}(4) = 	ext{QMA}(2)$) and the ability to simulate protocols using index purity gaps and Bell tests.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the general relationship between $	ext{QMA}(2; h)$ and $	ext{QMA}(2)$, then proving the logarithmic equivalence ($	ext{QMA}(2; O(\log n)) = 	ext{QMA}(2)$), and finally extending these results to the LOCC setting, where superlogarithmic entanglement implies $	ext{NP} \subseteq 	ext{BQP}$.
why_interesting: The results provide fundamental bounds on the role of entanglement in quantum complexity theory, which is crucial for understanding the limits of quantum verification protocols.
